reading.title: L5 Hospital 1: understanding the hospital
reading.text: At the hospital information desk, Leila asks about staff roles. The receptionist arranges visits and answers practical questions. A doctor examines patients, and a nurse supports their care. A surgeon performs operations. Before an operation, an anesthesiologist manages anesthesia and monitors the patient. A radiologist interprets medical images. Different specialists work with different body systems. Leila learns the names so she can understand who she will meet. The conversation does not tell her which specialist or treatment she needs. An ophthalmologist diagnoses and treats eye conditions. The guide identifies this as a medical specialist, not simply a person who sells glasses.

reading.title: L5 Hospital 2: understanding the hospital
reading.text: A visitor reads the hospital directory. Neurology concerns the nervous system, orthopedics concerns bones and joints, and ENT covers ears, nose, and throat. Oncology is the cancer service. The visitor waits in a waiting room until called. A lab technician works with samples in the laboratory. After an operation, patients may spend time in a recovery room while staff monitor them. The directory helps visitors understand names and locations; a qualified professional decides the appropriate care. An orthopedist specializes in bones and joints. An ENT specialist works with ears, nose, and throat; a urologist works with the urinary system; an oncologist works in cancer care. The operating room is where operations take place, and it is distinct from the recovery room.

reading.title: L5 Hospital 3: understanding the hospital
reading.text: The hospital guide explains its main areas. A consulting room is a private place to speak with a clinician. A maternity ward supports care around childbirth. The intensive care unit closely monitors people who are critically ill. At triage, staff assess urgency before arranging care. Equipment is processed in a sterilization room. The cafeteria serves meals for visitors and staff. Some areas have controlled access, so visitors ask staff where they may go rather than entering every room.
